newsitem.title: FRANCE: Glittering concert marks Rostropovich's birthday.
newsitem.headline: Glittering concert marks Rostropovich's birthday.

text.p: A prince, queens and government and business leaders surrounded cellist Mstislav Rostropovich as he celebrated his 70th birthday at a glittering concert on Thursday hosted by France's first lady.

Friends of the Russian maestro such as violinist Yehudi Menuhin performed for a celebrity audience including Britain's Prince Charles, Queens Sofia of Spain and Beatrix of the Netherlands and Italian Prime Minister Alberto Dini at Paris' Theatre des Champs-Elysees.
More than 400 pupils of Paris' music schools also attended the four-hour charity concert whose proceeds went to a Paris hospital foundation led by the wife of President Jacques Chirac, Bernadette.

Performers included violinists Isaac Stern and Gidon Kremer, pianist Van Cliburn, flutist Jean-Pierre Rampal and conductors Seiji Ozawa, Marcel Landowski and Semyon Bychkov and conductor-composer Krzysztof Penderecki.

With the London Symphony Orchestra, the Orchestre de Paris and the Orchestre National de France, they performed a European repertoire of works by Mozart, Haydn, Beethoven, Benjamin Britten, Prokoviev, Liszt, Schumann and Albeniz.

Rostropovich told Russia's Izvestia newspaper that he chose to mark his birthday in Paris because he could not accept a proposed state-funded celebration in Russia while his countrymen were in dire financial straits.
"I'd have been ashamed to show my face," he said.
Russian President Boris Yeltsin's contribution was to award the cellist an official honour "for services to the fatherland". Yeltsin's daughter Tatiana Diachenko attended the concert.
Stripped of his citizenship by the Soviet authorities in 1978, Rostropovich was rehabilitated by then President Mikhail Gorbachev in 1990.
He flew to Moscow in August 1991 to join Yeltsin's resistance to the hardline communist coup attempt and has since been a prominent campaigner for Yeltsin's democratic reforms.

Rostropovich, who divides his time between the United States, France and Russia, is regarded by music critics as still being at the height of his performing powers at an age when most people have retired. He is also a brilliant conductor and pianist.

Married to soprano Galina Vishnevskaya, he has performed around the world. In 1989, he rushed to Berlin to play his cello in joy at the opening of the Berlin Wall, symbolising the end of the East-West divide in Europe of which he was a victim.
